figures.title: One query's row: the shares mix the values
figures.caption: The softmax row is a mixture, not a choice. Each value vector is scaled by its share and the scaled vectors are laid head to tail: 0.665 v_1 + 0.245 v_2 + 0.090 v_3 ends at (0.755, 0.335). Both axes carry one scale, so a segment's length is its share times its vector's length.
figures.alt: A vector diagram with one scale on both axes. Three arrows lie head to tail from the origin: 0.665 v_1 runs along x to 0.665, 0.245 v_2 runs up the y axis to 0.245, and 0.090 v_3 runs diagonally to (0.755, 0.335). A dashed chord joins the origin to that endpoint. Beside the plot two rows print the arithmetic, x: 0.665·1 + 0.245·0 + 0.090·1 = 0.755 and y: 0.665·0 + 0.245·1 + 0.090·1 = 0.335.

data.scale: one scale on both axes; a segment's length is its share times its vector's length

anim.intro: Press Play or Next to score one query and mix the values.

steps.label: The top score takes share 0.665, so v_1 = (1, 0) contributes 0.665 along x.
Share 0.245 scales v_2 = (0, 1) to 0.245 up the y axis, added head to tail.
Share 0.090 scales v_3 = (1, 1) to 0.090 on both axes.
The path ends at (0.755, 0.335). The dashed chord is that sum; the rows beside it are its coordinates.

figures.title: Why divide by sqrt(d_k)
figures.caption: Score standard deviation against d_k under the paper's unit-variance assumption: the raw curve is sqrt(d_k), and the horizontal line is the scaled result, standard deviation 1. At d_k = 64 the raw standard deviation is 8, so a two-sigma gap between the top two scores gives an exponential ratio of about 8.9 million; dividing by sqrt(d_k) shrinks the gap by 8. The curve is computed from sqrt(d_k), not measured, and the gradient collapse lives in the note because it sits below the plot's range.
figures.alt: A log-log plot. The rising line is score standard deviation equal to square root of d_k, passing through d_k equals 1 with standard deviation 1, d_k equals 16 with 4, d_k equals 64 with 8, and d_k equals 4096 with 64. A horizontal line at standard deviation 1 is labelled after dividing by square root of d_k. A point at d_k equals 64, standard deviation 8 is labelled.

data.note: Under the assumption each product q_a k_a has variance 1, and the sum of d_k products has variance d_k, so the raw score standard deviation is sqrt(d_k). At d_k = 64 that is 8: a two-sigma gap gives an exponential ratio of e^16 ≈ 8.9 million, the top share is about 1 − e^−16, and its gradient a(1 − a) is about 1e−7. At a = 0.999 the gradient is 0.000999; at a = 0.665 it is 0.665 × 0.335 = 0.223, more than two hundred times larger. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) restores standard deviation 1 and shrinks the gap by 8.

anim.intro: Press Play or Next to follow the score spread down to a gradient.

steps.label: Each score sums d_k products of unit variance, so its standard deviation is sqrt(d_k).
At d_k = 64 the spread is 8. A two-sigma gap is e^16 ≈ 8.9 million to one.
That saturates softmax: the top share is about 1 − e^−16 and its gradient about 1e−7.
Dividing by sqrt(d_k) puts the spread back at 1 and shrinks the gap by 8.

figures.title: One layer's score matrix at 100,000 tokens
figures.caption: The score matrix is what the quadratic cost buys. At n = 100,000 one head holds 10^10 entries, 20 GB in 16-bit precision; all 32 heads at once would be 640 GB, more than three times the 192 GB an H100 holds. Real implementations tile the computation, so the full matrix never materialises.
figures.alt: One bar drawn to scale from 0 to 640 GB. A fill covers the whole bar, labelled 32 heads: 640 GB. Inside it a reserved span reaches 192 GB, labelled H100: 192 GB. A narrow share at the left end is 20 GB, the score matrix for one head, labelled below the bar because the span is too narrow to hold text. The axis marks 0, 192 GB and 640 GB.

data.note: At n = 100,000 the score matrix holds n^2 = 10^10 pairs. Per layer the attention arithmetic is 4 n^2 d_model = 4 × 10^10 × 4096 ≈ 1.6 × 10^14 FLOPs, 160 trillion. One head's scores in 16-bit precision are 10^10 entries × 2 bytes = 20 GB; 32 heads would need 640 GB. Since 640 GB is more than three times 192 GB, implementations tile the computation and never hold the full matrix.

anim.intro: Press Play or Next to build the matrix that never fits.

steps.label: One head at 100,000 tokens: 10^10 entries, 20 GB in fp16.
An H100 holds 192 GB. One head's scores already take a tenth of it.
All 32 heads at once would be 640 GB: more than three times the card.
So the matrix is tiled. The arithmetic is real; the array never is.
